scenes.text: 3 products. 6 upload sheets each. 1 command. And an assistant your team can ask. This is supplier catalogue automation, built for FCI London.
By hand, the Richard bed means finding it in a 373-page price list, then typing 2,340 price rows.
Here, the suppliers' own files go in: Cattelan's PDF price list, and Franco Ferri's spreadsheet and swatch card. A short job file names the product, and 1 command does the rest.

Richard's page holds 70 prices: 5 sizes, 10 cover columns, and a storage version. Cattelan's online catalogue supplies the 356 colours behind those columns. So 70 prices become 2,340 rows, copied exactly.
Burt is modular, so each layout is the sum of its modules. 698, plus 320, plus 564, plus 731: £2,313.

Photos stay at the supplier's full resolution, cropped square and saved with the supplier's own JPEG settings. Measured against the originals, every photo scores between 56 and 65 decibels: visually identical, even zoomed in.
Cattelan's swatches are downloaded. Franco Ferri publishes none, so the tool reuses the 162 FCI already hosts, and lists the 34 still needed.
NVIDIA's Nemotron writes the descriptions from the supplier's facts, and each one is checked before it's used.
To test it, I added Thomas, a bed FCI built by hand. Every size matches, the base price matches FCI's live page, and it found 41 colours FCI still lists that Cattelan no longer offers.

The team works in Google Drive. Price lists go in a folder, and products are rows in a sheet. A new catalogue is picked up by its name, with no setup change, and every result is saved back to Drive, by date.
Each run compares every price with the last one, and writes only the rows that changed, ready to upload. Re-running Thomas: 560 unchanged.
And anyone can just ask. The assistant answers from the run results, never from memory. Richard, size D, in glove leather: 3 prices, each checked against the data.
Asking it to re-run a product only proposes the run. Nothing happens until someone presses Confirm. Then it re-prices from Drive, and saves the results back.
Anything a person should check goes into a report. One command folds the rows back into the 70 prices on the PDF page for a quick hand check, and 192 tests run on every push.
85 to 90 percent of the work, automated. A new product is a row in a sheet, and a new supplier is a new reader.
Designed and built by Prateek Sahni. Scan the QR code to visit his website, and explore more of his work.
